Juvenile individuals of Gracilechinus affinis emerge from the egg with a test diameter of merely 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm], a remarkably small size that reflects the minimal maternal provisioning typical of planktotrophic echinoderm larvae. The corresponding wet weight at this earliest post-settlement stage is approximately 0.000002 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000002 grams], a value that underscores the severe energetic constraints faced by newly metamorphosed recruits on the seafloor. Field surveys conducted in the North Atlantic have reported that these tiny juveniles grow slowly during their first few months, gradually developing the skeletal plates that will eventually define their adult morphology. The initial vulnerability of such diminutive individuals is thought to drive exceptionally high rates of early mortality, as predation pressure from benthic invertebrates is intense. Despite this precarious beginning, survivors that successfully navigate the bottleneck of early juvenile life can persist for many years, provided they find adequate shelter and food resources on the rocky substrata they typically inhabit.

The most reliable estimates of growth and maturation in Gracilechinus affinis come from a long-term laboratory study conducted at a stable water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. Under these cold conditions, typical of their deep-water habitat, the time required to reach sexual maturity from the point of settlement is 2000 days from the point of settlement [tp = 2000 days from the point of settlement] at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. This protracted developmental period is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many deep-sea echinoids, where low metabolic rates and limited food availability delay the onset of gametogenesis. At the moment of puberty, the test diameter averages 1.6 cm [Lp = 1.6 cm], and the concomitant wet weight is recorded at 1.0 gram [Wwp = 1.0 gram]. The transition from juvenile to reproductively capable adult thus represents a roughly eighty-fold increase in linear dimension from birth, and an even more dramatic five-hundred-thousand-fold increase in mass, highlighting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive effort can commence.

As Gracilechinus affinis continues its slow growth beyond puberty, individuals approach an asymptotic test diameter of 5.5 cm [Li = 5.5 cm], which represents the maximum shell size attained by fully grown adults in natural populations. The ultimate wet weight associated with this maximal dimension is 37.0 grams [Wwi = 37.0 grams], a body mass that positions this species as an intermediate-sized member of the echinoid community on the continental slope. Comparative analyses with congeneric species such as Gracilechinus acutus and Gracilechinus elegans reveal that the asymptotic size of Gracilechinus affinis falls near the lower end of the genus range, likely reflecting adaptations to the colder, more food-limited environments it occupies. The allometric relationship between test diameter and wet weight in this species follows the standard cubic scaling law, with fully hydrated individuals achieving a tissue density that is consistent with other regular echinoids from similar depths. This maximum body size is not achieved until well after the onset of sexual maturity.

The maximum recorded longevity of Gracilechinus affinis, documented in the same long-term laboratory cohort at a stable 5 °C [T = 5 °C], reaches 11000 days [am = 11000 days], which is equivalent to approximately three decades. This remarkable lifespan is among the longest documented for any regular echinoid, rivaling that of certain deep-water species such as Strongylocentrotus franciscanus. The slow pace of life in this species is further reflected in the extended interval between puberty and the age of natural death, which spans nearly 9000 days, during which individuals presumably engage in multiple annual spawning events. Such extreme longevity is thought to be an evolutionary response to unpredictable recruitment conditions in deep-sea environments, where favorable settlement years are rare and adults must persist through long periods of low food availability. The constant low temperature is believed to slow the accumulation of oxidative damage, thereby extending both the reproductive window and the total lifespan.

At the onset of reproductive activity, gravid adult females of Gracilechinus affinis release their gametes into the water column during synchronized spawning events that are likely triggered by seasonal phytoplankton blooms reaching the benthos. The time since birth at puberty, calculated under a stable thermal regime of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], has been precisely measured at 2000 days since birth [tp = 2000 days since birth], a value that marks the point at which resources begin to be directed toward gonad development. This delayed maturation contrasts sharply with the life history of shallow-water congeners, which often reach sexual maturity within one to two years, and likely reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by the perpetually cold deep-sea environment. The ecological trade-off is clear: by deferring reproduction for more than five years, individuals attain a larger body size that enhances both competitive ability and fecundity per spawning event, thereby maximizing lifetime reproductive output in an environment where reproductive opportunities are stochastic.
